name: Yusuf Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Yusuf. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties. Everything here is confidential, so feel free to tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I lead a transmission crew, so the big steel towers that carry high voltage across the farmland, the ones people see from the motorway and never think about. A normal day, we drive out from the yard at Harlow Flats, set up, climb, and spend the day replacing insulators or fixing damper weights on the conductors, which are the big cables. Some of those towers are sixty metres, and up there the wind is a different animal.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's honest work you can see. You fix a tower, it stands for another forty years. What wears me out is the travel, sometimes two hours each way in the crew truck, and the money, because we're on the regional rate, which is lower than the city crews get for the exact same climb.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who's at home when you get back?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Ana, my girlfriend. She's in her second year of nursing school, so I'm covering most of the rent and her bus pass, which is why the bank account is always flat by the twentieth. We've got a deal that once she qualifies, she pays me back in holidays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say well, there you go, it's a smarter spreadsheet. At work the guys would laugh about all the money spent on those talks the company made us sit through. Online I might share a cartoon about it, nothing serious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it'd be fine for me. I use a chatbot now and then to tidy up my incident reports, because writing isn't my thing, and that would carry on. My job would be the same climb, the same pay, and the same fight for a better regional rate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am and keep my union dues paid, because the pay gap with the city crews is the real issue. I'd try to put something aside once Ana starts earning in two years. Maybe I'd do the extra rescue training course in spring because it pays a small allowance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Bit bored, maybe, because nothing changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you use a chatbot for reports. How did you start with that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marta, who climbs with me, showed me after I spent a whole evening on one report about a dropped shackle. She typed in my notes and it came out in proper sentences in a minute. I checked every line, mind you, because if it says something wrong, it's my name on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the first thing you'd spend money on, if it stayed normal and money got a bit easier?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: New boots, honestly, mine are held together with tape at the heel. Then a weekend away with Ana by the sea, which we keep promising each other.

S0.say: I'd say it's just a smarter spreadsheet and the guys would laugh about the money spent on the company's AI talks. Online I'd maybe share a cartoon about it.
S0.think: It would be fine for me, because I'd still use a chatbot now and then for reports and the climbing stays the same. The real fight would stay the regional pay rate.
S0.do: Keeps working as normal, keeps paying union dues and keeps pushing for a better regional rate. Takes the spring rescue training course for its small allowance and plans to save once his girlfriend starts earning.
S0.feel: Calm and a little bored that nothing changes.
S0.quote: My job would be the same climb, the same pay, and the same fight for a better regional rate.
S0.fieldNote: Yusuf is easy-going and practical, and he already uses AI in a small, careful way for reports. He checks every line because his name is on it. Money is tight mainly because he's supporting his girlfriend through nursing school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's coming whether we like it or not, so the union had better be at the table early. Drones already do some of our inspections, and I'd say fine, as long as the people who used to walk those lines get first dibs on the drone jobs. I'd say that on the crew group chat too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd be all right. Nobody's building a robot that can swap a cracked insulator on a sixty-metre tower in a crosswind any time soon. The bit that worries me is the planning and the paperwork side shrinking, because that's where the easier jobs are when your knees go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait a few months to see what the company actually brings in, because they announce a lot and do half. Once the drone pilot course is running and a couple of people have done it, I'd sign up, ideally on company time. And I'd push the union rep to get a clause that anyone retrained keeps their grade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm. A small itch in the back of my head about later on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait to see. What would convince you it's real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I saw them actually cut the walking patrols in another region, not just talk about it. Or if Ian, my supervisor, started asking who wants the drone course. When Ian asks, it's real, because he hates wasting a training budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The older guys in the planning office, like Rob, who came off the towers after a back injury. If the AI does the job planning, where does the next Rob go when his back gives out?

S1.say: I'd say it's coming whether we like it or not, so the union needs to be at the table early. People who used to walk the lines should get first dibs on the drone jobs.
S1.think: I think I'd be all right, because no robot is swapping insulators on a sixty-metre tower in a crosswind soon. What worries me is losing the office and planning jobs people move into when their bodies wear out.
S1.do: Waits a few months to see what the company really brings in, then signs up for the drone pilot course once others have done it. Pushes his union rep for a clause that retrained workers keep their grade.
S1.feel: Mostly calm, with a small worry in the back of his mind about later years.
S1.quote: When Ian asks, it's real, because he hates wasting a training budget.
S1.fieldNote: His approach is to wait for proof and then move, and his test for proof is very concrete. He's less worried about his own climbing job than about the softer office jobs that injured lineworkers rely on. His progressive views show up in his concern for older colleagues.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs the government, full stop. A change this big in two years, you need wage protection and retraining money from the state, not just whatever the company feels like giving. I'd be out on the street with the union if it came to that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd be in real trouble. Ana wouldn't have qualified yet, I've got nothing saved, and if the company could suddenly buy a robot that climbs, they'd start with transmission because it's the most dangerous and the most expensive to insure. My whole plan was to carry us both for two years and then breathe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Week one, I'd sit down with Ana and go through every cost, and we'd cancel the car insurance on her old hatchback and sell it. I'd take every overtime shift I can get while the work's still there, and put every spare bit into savings. I'd join whatever action the union calls, and I'd ask the company straight out what the retraining offer is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like the tower's swaying and you can't see the bottom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change any plans with Ana?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd talked about moving in together properly next year, into a bigger place. That would stop. If it got bad, we'd move in with her parents on the edge of town, which they'd be kind about and I'd hate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the short warning time take away from you, specifically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The two years I was counting on. Ana qualifying was supposed to be the moment we had two wages. With AGI by 2028, it lands right in the middle of that, before we've got anything under us.

S2.say: This needs the government, full stop, with wage protection and retraining money from the state. I'd be out on the street with the union if it came to that.
S2.think: I think I'd be in real trouble, with Ana not yet qualified and nothing saved. If robots could climb, they'd start with transmission work because it's the most dangerous and costly to insure.
S2.do: Goes through every cost with his girlfriend in the first week and sells her old car. Takes every overtime shift, saves every spare bit, joins union action and asks the company directly what the retraining offer is.
S2.feel: Alarmed, like a swaying tower where you can't see the bottom.
S2.quote: Like the tower's swaying and you can't see the bottom.
S2.fieldNote: The fast scenario hits exactly when he's carrying two people on one low wage. He expects transmission to be targeted first because of insurance costs, which surprised me. His public line is about the state, while privately the fear is about the timing with Ana's studies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to do it fairly, so there's no excuse for chaos. The union and the government should agree a plan now. I'd say that at work, and I'd probably sign every petition going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years helps a lot. Ana would be qualified and working, nurses would still be needed for a while, and we'd have two wages. I'd still lose the climbing eventually, but I'd have a chance to move into something before the cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd do the drone and remote inspection courses as soon as they're offered, and I'd ask about the robot maintenance side, because someone has to fix the things. I'd start saving once Ana's earning, aiming for three months by year three. I'd vote for whoever promises a proper retraining fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but more in control. I can see the steps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said nurses would still be needed for a while. Does that change who earns in your house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, and I'm fine with that. My dad would have hated the idea of his wife earning more, but I'm not him. If Ana carries us for a bit while I retrain, that's fair, I carried her first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you be doing in year four or five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hope to be a technician on the robot crews, the person who goes up when the machine gets stuck or does something stupid. I'd have proven I can learn it by then, because I'd have started early enough to not be the last in line.

S3.say: Five years is enough time to do this fairly, so there's no excuse for chaos. The union and the government should agree a plan now, and I'd sign every petition going.
S3.think: Five years helps a lot, because Ana would be qualified and we'd have two wages. I'd still lose the climbing in the end, but I'd have a chance to move before the cliff.
S3.do: Takes the drone and remote inspection courses as soon as they're offered and asks about robot maintenance work. Starts saving once his girlfriend earns, aiming for three months by year three, and votes for a retraining fund.
S3.feel: Anxious but more in control, because he can see the steps ahead.
S3.quote: My dad would have hated the idea of his wife earning more, but I'm not him.
S3.fieldNote: The five-year gap changes everything for him because it lines up with his girlfriend qualifying. He's happy for her to be the main earner for a while, which he frames as fairness. He aims to become the technician who rescues stuck robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years I'd say this is a chance to make the job safer, if we do it right. Nobody should have to die falling off a tower, and if a robot takes the worst climbs, good. But I'd say the workers have to share in what it saves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years feels manageable. I'd be thirty-seven, with time to learn the new side properly while still climbing, and Ana would be well into her career. It's the kind of change I like, slow enough to see who it works for before I jump.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on climbing for now and watch which companies are using robot crews well. In a couple of years, once it's proven, I'd go for the robot technician training, and I'd put a little aside every month into savings once Ana's working. I'd keep pushing the union for a share of the savings to go into wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy at the back, but mostly fine. It feels like weather I can plan around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned someone falling. Is that from experience?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A guy from the next region, Pete, fell two years ago when a step bolt gave way. He lived, but he walks with a stick now. So when people say robots are scary, I think of Pete, and I think some of this could be good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does ten years give you that two years doesn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to be the second one through the door, which is how I like it. With two years there's no second, everyone's running at once. With ten I can watch, learn and then move.

S4.say: With ten years this could make the job safer if we do it right, and if robots take the worst climbs, good. But workers have to share in what it saves.
S4.think: Ten years feels manageable, because I'd have time to learn the new side while still climbing and Ana would be well into her career. It's slow enough to see who it works for before I jump.
S4.do: Keeps climbing for now and watches which companies use robot crews well. Goes for robot technician training once it's proven, saves a little each month, and pushes the union for a share of the savings in wages.
S4.feel: Mostly fine, with a little unease in the background, like weather he can plan around.
S4.quote: So when people say robots are scary, I think of Pete, and I think some of this could be good.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, his steady temperament fits perfectly: he wants to be second through the door. His friend Pete's fall makes him see real safety benefits in robots. He still insists workers share in the savings.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it lands before Ana qualifies and before we've saved anything. What would help is a proper wage guarantee while you retrain, paid for by the companies that save money on robots, not just some online course and a handshake.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the danger. Everyone talks about losing jobs, but nobody asks the people who climb these things whether we'd mind not risking our necks. I climb sixty-metre towers for a living, and the scariest height I know is the bottom of my bank account.

headlineQuote: I climb sixty-metre towers for a living, and the scariest height I know is the bottom of my bank account.
portrait: Yusuf Ziegler is a 27-year-old transmission crew leader who climbs high-voltage towers across farmland on a lower regional pay rate. He's carrying most of the bills while his girlfriend Ana finishes nursing school, so he has almost nothing saved. He uses AI now and then for reports and likes to move once a change is proven. The slow scenarios leave him calm, the two-year AGI picture alarms him because of its timing, and with five or ten years he plans to retrain as a technician on robot crews, happy for Ana to earn more for a while.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because it would arrive before Ana qualifies as a nurse and before they've saved anything.
whatWouldHelp: A real wage guarantee while workers retrain, paid for by the companies that save money on robots, rather than an online course and a handshake.
